At defaults it is competent but generic. It matches what free wave generators already produce, with little to distinguish it for paying professionals.
grades.lesson: Build colour ramps from brand inputs by stepping lightness and chroma, not by interpolating hue between distant colours. Clamp every range knob so its maximum still renders as a deliberate design, never a muddy or mechanical artefact.

brief: Seamless herringbone tile pattern. Knobs: plank length and width, angle, grout gap, color variation per plank, and palette. Price: 0

flaws: Dark brand probe is garish. The planks are pushed to acid chartreuse/lime against pure black grout with heavy bevel outlines, so it reads like dated clip art, not a tile surface. The dark brand is applied as near-black grout and the accent at full saturation, with no tonal control.
Light brand probe mixes saturated teal planks with flat, desaturated grey-taupe planks. The per-plank variation reads as dirty or mismatched tiles instead of a natural glaze spread.
The bevel and highlight shading is generic and slightly plasticky. In the Oak preset it gives wood a moulded, toy-like look rather than parquet.
The angle knob shows no visible effect in any render, including the all-max render, which keeps the same 45° layout. Either the range is too timid or the knob is not meaningfully exposed.
At all-max, the planks become so long and wide relative to the canvas that only about two rows of the herringbone remain. It reads more as a zoomed crop than a usable pattern at that scale.
Commodity subject. A plain herringbone with a bevel adds little over the free textures designers already have, and nothing in the renders sets it apart.
grades.lesson: When mapping brand colours into a material pattern, derive every surface tone from the brand hue but clamp saturation and lightness into a believable range for that material. Never drop the raw brand colour or pure black/white straight onto fills, grout, or outlines; dark brands especially need lifted mid-tones, not neon on black.

flaws: Dark brand probe does not read as a dark brand. It renders as a saturated lime-green tile with heavy black outlines. The per-plank variation collapses into a crude two-tone light/mid stripe, which looks cartoonish and cheap next to the restrained defaults.
Light brand probe pushes the teal to high saturation with stark white grout. It is loud and loses the soft ceramic-glaze quality the defaults have.

At every range knob's maximum, the very long, thin planks plus the off-axis angle and wide grout weaken the herringbone geometry. Several zigzag junctions look misaligned or cramped, and the composition reads as scattered sticks rather than a laid floor.
At maximum, colour variation produces a blotchy mix of pale and dark planks. Mottled noise also bleeds into the wide grout, so the grout looks dirty rather than intentional.
Rotating to arbitrary angles raises a seamlessness risk that cannot be confirmed from the renders. Nothing shows the tile edges still match at non-axis angles.

The palette handling is inconsistent. Oak gets dark grout and a flat cel-shaded look, while the ceramic presets get white grout and glaze streaks. The presets feel like different assets rather than one coherent system.
Usefulness is limited. Herringbone backgrounds are niche in product UI work, and the defaults are competent but generic, comparable to free stock textures.
grades.lesson: When a brand colour drives a generated palette, derive the base, variation and grout tones in a perceptual colour space anchored to the input's lightness. Clamp chroma and the variation spread so any input, especially dark ones, keeps its value character and never turns neon or two-tone. Then check the result at combined extremes, not just one knob at a time.

brief: Isometric triangle or dot grid with optional extruded cubes. Knobs: cell size, line or dot mode, cube density, shading palette, and random seed. Price: 4

flaws: Unbalanced composition at defaults. The cube clusters bunch in the upper-left and centre, leaving the lower-left quarter and the right edge empty. It reads as random scatter rather than a placed pattern, and a designer cannot drop it behind content without the weight feeling off.

Cluster shapes look like arbitrary fragments, not deliberate forms. The bottom-left cluster in particular has a top face that seems to float or bleed past its cube, so it reads as a depth-sorting glitch.
The 'Linen' preset renders pixel-identical to the defaults. One of the only two presets adds no variety.

At every range knob's maximum, the asset stops being a pattern. A few oversized chunky blocks fill the frame, the grid is barely visible, and the flat orange tile has ambiguous depth that reads as a hole or an error. Cell size and density at max should produce a denser field, not a zoomed-in crop.
Dot mode, one of the five briefed knobs, never appears in any render, so its quality cannot be verified.
The shading is a fixed three-tone ramp of the brand colour. There is no control over light direction or face contrast, which limits how well it can match an existing illustration system.
grades.lesson: When placing procedural elements, distribute them with an explicit balance rule across the full canvas, such as Poisson spacing or quadrant weighting. Never let raw random seeds decide composition, because unseeded clustering is what makes generative assets read as accidental rather than designed.

flaws: Default composition is a flat, evenly spaced scatter of eight isolated blocks with no clustering, no scale hierarchy and no focal area. It reads as placeholder clip art rather than a designed pattern or illustration.
The asset falls between two uses. The cubes are too saturated and prominent to sit behind content as a background, and too sparse and generic to carry a layout as an illustration.
Cube density at maximum does not produce a denser field. The max render still shows only eight shapes, now in a rigid 4x2 grid with larger cells, so the knob reads as mislabelled or ineffective.
Blocks are tightly packed in the max render. The top-left orange cluster nearly touches its neighbour, and the bottom-left orange shape crowds the blue one beside it.
Shape vocabulary is very limited: single cubes, columns, stairs and L-shapes. The same handful repeats across every render.

In the dark brand probe the grid lines are bright and dense enough to create a busy moiré-like texture that competes with the cubes. The light brand probe grid is also noticeably heavier than the defaults.
Dot mode, one of the briefed knobs, is not demonstrated in any render, so its quality cannot be verified.
grades.lesson: A density or count knob must visibly change coverage across its range. Render the min, mid and max values side by side, and if max does not look clearly fuller than default, the knob is broken regardless of what other parameters it moves.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A round plaza fountain on a 4x4 footprint: stepped stone basin, central column, water as pale blue cylinders. Knobs: stone colour, water colour, tiers 1-3, size.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: lights

flaws: Light brand probe maps the brand colour onto the water, producing a coral/red fountain that reads as lava or blood rather than water. A semantically fixed material was hijacked by the brand accent.

Dark brand probe turns the stone near-black. The faceted basin sides lose almost all face shading and read as flat black slabs, while the outer plinth stays white, so the piece looks half-themed and mismatched.
Water jets are thin, opaque, evenly spaced vertical rods with no arc, spray or splash. They read as support poles or railings, not falling water.
The 'size' knob barely changes the footprint between default and max. It is unclear what it controls, and it cannot be verified against the 4x4 grid footprint in the brief.
At defaults the asset fills under half the frame, leaving large dead space and making small details (lamps, lily pads, spout) hard to read at thumbnail size.
Corner lamps and lily pads ignore every palette and brand probe. They are fine in isolation but become visually disconnected in the slate, terracotta and dark renders.
The spire option is a plain orange cone in the accent colour, which clashes with the stone palette and looks like a traffic cone rather than a finial.
grades.lesson: When a brand or theme colour drives recolouring, map it only to accent and trim parts. Keep semantically fixed materials (water, foliage, skin, glass) within a believable hue range. Also clamp surface lightness so dark themes still show face-to-face shading on 3D forms.

flaws: The default top spray is a cluster of tiny pale rods. At this scale it reads as noisy stubble, not a water plume, and it is the weakest part of the silhouette.
Water jets are drawn as opaque, evenly lit cylinders with hard white discs at their bases. They read as glass posts standing in the basin rather than falling water.
At max range, the third tier is a small cap on a thin stem. Jets from three rims crisscross the lower basins, making the middle of the model busy and hard to read.

The size knob grows the basin but not the plaza or the lamp positions. At max, the outer basin nearly fills the square plinth, the walkway margin all but disappears, and the front lamp sits almost against the basin wall.

The plinth renders at a noticeably different screen scale at max than at defaults. For a kit piece that must match town-shop.mjs on a 6 m grid, the footprint and on-screen scale should stay locked, and the size knob does not respect that.
There are no knobs for lamps (on/off, count) or for jet density. These are the controls a designer placing this in a town scene would reach for before tier count.
grades.lesson: When a size or count knob grows the main form, scale or reposition the dependent elements (surrounds, props, margins) with it, and check the max render for crowding against the fixed footprint, not just for clipping.

flaws: The 'water' jets are faceted hexagonal prisms with pointed tips. They read as ice or quartz crystals, not water, and contradict the brief's 'pale blue cylinders'. At every render this looks like a crystal fountain, not a plaza water feature.
The central column does not read. The spire finial sits on a ring that appears to float above the upper-basin disc, with no visible shaft connecting them.
The upper basin is centred on a flat orange disc (cyan in the dark probe) that looks like a coin or pad, not water or stone. The accent colour is misapplied to a water surface.
The Travertine preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it is a wasted preset slot.
At maximum, the stacked tiers become a cluttered wedding cake. Extra jets crowd the rims and visually collide with tier edges, and the front lamp post overlaps the basin silhouette.
The size knob has little visible effect at maximum. The basin grows slightly while the plaza and lamps stay fixed, so the knob's purpose is unclear.
Lamp posts are not in the brief. They are hardwired, and their warm glow clashes with the cyan or green accents in the dark probe and the Slate preset.
In Slate, the lily pads go grey-beige on mint water and nearly disappear.
grades.lesson: When the brief names a material and a primitive (e.g. 'water as pale blue cylinders'), build that literal form. Then check at thumbnail size that the shape cues read as that substance: flat sheets and rounded jets for water, not faceted, pointed prisms that read as crystal. A stylised substitute that changes what the object appears to be is a brief failure, not a style choice.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A bookshop with a green front, shelves of coloured book spines in the window and a hanging sign. Knobs: front colour, book colours seed, floors 1-3, lights.

flaws: The dark brand probe breaks the asset. The walls go pure black and the roof goes near-white, so the roof planes lose almost all shading separation. The building reads as an inverted silhouette, not a town shop.
In the dark brand probe the fascia lettering turns cyan on lime green and is illegible. The trim and shopfront go to a harsh acid lime that clashes with the rest of the kit palette.

The fascia sign text is tiny pixel lettering that reads as 'BOC', not a recognisable word, even at defaults. The signage element meant to identify the bookshop is not legible at any render size shown.
Preset 'Evergreen' renders pixel-identical to the defaults, so it adds no value as a preset.
The brand mapping routes brand colour onto the wall masses and roof rather than limiting it to trim, shopfront and accents. Any dark brand therefore swamps the whole building.
The hanging sign is a small blob whose icon cannot be read at any size shown. It barely registers as a hanging sign.
The window book spines are a noisy jumble at this scale and do not clearly read as shelves of books in the side window.
grades.lesson: When mapping brand colours onto an illustration, apply them only to accent surfaces such as trim, signage and doors. Keep large masses such as walls and roofs on a fixed neutral palette. Derive every text colour by checking contrast against its actual background, so an extreme brand colour can never invert the object or make its label unreadable.

flaws: The fascia lettering is broken in every render. The blocky glyphs read as 'E:OC' or 'B:DC', not a real word such as 'BOOKS'. Garbled text on the hero sign is the first thing a viewer reads and makes the asset unusable as a branded shop.
The glyphs change between renders (E:OC, then BDC at max floors). This suggests the lettering is built from procedural blocks that do not form letters reliably.
The hanging sign is a tiny, unreadable smudge at the 512 render size and adds no identity. It should carry a clear book icon or be scaled up.
The side shop window shows mostly uniform blue spines at defaults. That contradicts the brief's 'shelves of coloured book spines', and the variety only shows on the front window.

The dark brand probe produces a bright lime front, a periwinkle roof and grey walls. Nothing about it reads as dark, and the lime clashes with the warm house palette, so brand-colour mapping is not tuned for a dark brand.
The defaults mix unlit grey and lit yellow windows with no clear logic, e.g. a single grey side window next to all-lit front windows. It looks accidental rather than art-directed.
The base massing, roof options, floors knob and front colour presets (Oxford, Plum) are solid and stay coherent, including the flat-roof variant. Text is the blocker.
grades.lesson: Never hand-assemble lettering from primitive blocks unless every glyph has been checked at the final render size. Either use a vetted glyph set, or replace text with a clear pictogram, because illegible signage reads as broken and sinks an otherwise good asset.

flaws: Dark brand probe: the roof and walls take the brand, but the shopfront stays at the default green. The asset's signature element ignores the brand, so the result looks half-themed. The light probe, by contrast, recolours the front to teal.
Dark brand probe: the walls go a cold blue-grey and the menu plaque turns a stray cyan. The warm town palette the brief asks for is lost, and the building reads as concrete.

The flat-roof variant renders noticeably larger, with a wider footprint, than the pitched variants. Either the framing auto-fits or the geometry changes. Either way it undermines the 'matching town-shop.mjs scale on the 6 m grid' requirement for a kit piece.
There is no legible entrance. The right of the shopfront is a blank green slab and the dark corner pilaster is ambiguous, so the bookshop has no readable door.
At max floors, the book spines darken and muddy under the reseeded colours, losing the bright coloured-spines read that sells the window.
The 'lights' knob is not demonstrated. Every render shows identical lit yellow windows, so its effect cannot be verified.
grades.lesson: Map brand colours to fixed roles, such as front, roof, trim and wall, and apply that mapping the same way for every brand. If a brand colour fails a contrast or legibility check, shift its lightness within that role. Never silently fall back to the default hue for the hero element while recolouring the rest.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A corner cafe with a glass front, two outdoor tables with parasols and chairs on the pavement side (z 0 to 1.5). Knobs: wall, parasol colour, tables 0-3, floors 1-2, lights.

flaws: Dark brand probe breaks the building. Walls go near-black, the roof and rooftop unit go flat white, and the roof nearly disappears against the light canvas, so the silhouette dissolves.
Dark brand probe also brings in a saturated cyan fascia and lime awnings and parasols that clash with the town palette. This piece would not sit next to town-shop.mjs.
In the dark brand probe the glass front washes out to a pale peach, which kills the 'glass front' read that defines the asset.

At every range knob maximum, three tables and parasols crowd a pavement strip sized for two. Parasol canopies overlap each other and the awning, chairs stack together, and the corner planter and bin get buried.
The max-knobs render looks the same as defaults apart from the table count. The lights knob and floors knob produce no visible change, so those knobs are either inert or not legible.
The rooftop unit stays white in every preset and probe and is never themed. On the Bistro roof it reads as a pasted-on block.
Parasols at default sit tight under the awnings. In the iso view, canopy and awning edges nearly collide, which makes the shopfront busy.
grades.lesson: Map brand colours to surfaces by role with luminance guards. Large surfaces like roofs and walls should get desaturated, clamped tints of the brand colour rather than the raw value. Every major mass should keep visible contrast against both the canvas and its neighbouring faces. Check this in both the light and dark brand probes before submitting.

flaws: Dark brand probe washes out the brand accent. The parasols turn near-white cream and disappear against the white pavement. The awning stripes become pale lime on white with almost no contrast. A cyan fascia band appears above the awning that exists in no other render. The 'dark' brand also yields a light periwinkle roof, so the brand mapping is not behaving predictably.

At every range knob maxed, the third table and parasol are packed into the same fixed pavement strip. The parasols crowd each other and nearly collide with the awning. The chairs overlap and the tables press against the glass front. The pavement does not grow, and table spacing does not adapt to the count.
With roof set to gable, the roof eave comes down onto the awning and appears to clip its top edge. The awning and roof were not reconciled for this option.
The brief says corner cafe with a glass front, but the side elevation is a plain wall with an ordinary window. Only one face reads as the cafe front, so the corner condition is not sold.
At defaults, the awning's white end cap projects past the building corner into empty air, which reads as a modelling slip rather than a deliberate wrap.
Parasol colour and awning colour appear locked together. There is no visible independent lights state among the renders, so it is unclear whether the 'lights' knob does anything meaningful.
The 1 to 2 floors range works, but the upper-floor windows are small and sparse relative to the wide ground floor. The two-storey version looks top-light.
grades.lesson: When one brand colour drives several elements, derive each tint with a minimum contrast against the surfaces it sits on, such as white stripes, pavement and walls. Check this in both light and dark brand probes rather than applying a fixed lighten or darken step.

flaws: Second table set is jammed against the facade beside the door at defaults. Its parasol canopy butts into the awning line and its table and chairs are hidden, so the brief's 'two outdoor tables with chairs' reads as one table plus a stray parasol.
At max tables the rear parasols crowd the shopfront and overlap the awning edge instead of sitting out on the pavement band (z 0 to 1.5).
The yellow fascia/sign band above the glazing is mostly hidden behind the awning in every render. The signage detail is wasted and the top of the facade looks cluttered.
With 'roof' set to 'gable', the eave drops onto the awning and crushes the sign band. The ends also read as a hip on one side and an unresolved slope on the other, not a clean gable.
Awning valance corner is chunky and jagged where the two runs meet, with blocky protrusions rather than a clean mitre.
Parasol colour does not follow the palette sensibly. Bistro gets cold lilac-grey parasols against its red and brown scheme, and the dark brand probe gets pale lime parasols unrelated to the brand.
The dark brand probe renders the roof as a washed-out periwinkle rather than a dark tone. It is nearly indistinguishable from the Harbour preset, so the probe adds no real range.
Glazing is a flat orange-yellow fill in every render. The 'lights' knob has no visible effect in any render, so its value cannot be confirmed.
grades.lesson: Whenever a knob adds, moves or swaps geometry (roof type, extra floors, prop counts), recompute clearances against every attached facade element (awnings, signage, doors) instead of reusing fixed offsets. Then render each variant to confirm nothing collides with or hides another element.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A bakery with a big bread-shaped sign, a bay window of loaves, a striped awning and a chimney. Knobs: wall, awning (primary role), sign colour, floors 1-3, chimney toggle, lights.

flaws: The bakery identity is weak at defaults. The 'big bread-shaped sign' reads as a jumble of orange blocks on top of the awning, not a loaf. The bay window of loaves is not legible. The shopfront is a small, cluttered corner on what otherwise reads as a generic two-storey house.

The white floor slabs cut across the wall faces between storeys, giving a cutaway or dollhouse look. They read as a construction error rather than a deliberate cornice, and get more obvious at 3 floors.
Preset 'Brioche' is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it adds nothing.
Dark brand probe: the bread sign turns saturated cyan, which destroys the one element meant to say 'bakery'.
Dark brand probe: the roof goes pure white, reading as snow.
Dark brand probe: the walls go pure black, with the left and right faces losing all isometric shading so the volume flattens.
Dark brand probe: the lime awning clashes with the rest of the palette.
Light brand probe: the sign washes out to near-white and loses contrast against the white awning stripes and slab.
Light brand probe: the shadowed roof face goes almost black against teal, which is out of step with the soft palette elsewhere.
Lit windows at max floors are a random mix of amber and slate. There is no evident 'lights' control intent.
The sign colour knob is allowed to drive a food object to colours no bread can be, and brand colour bleeds into it. The knobs need semantic constraints.
grades.lesson: Separate brand-driven colour roles from semantically fixed objects (food, skin, materials like brick). For every brand-mapped role, clamp lightness so faces keep their isometric value steps and stay distinct from neighbours. Then verify the hero element still reads as itself under both a very light and a very dark brand.

flaws: The bakery identity, which is the whole point of the asset, does not read. The 'big bread-shaped sign' looks like a stack of planks or a crate lid, not a loaf, and the 'bay window of loaves' is a few illegible brown dots behind the awning.

The shopfront is a cluttered pile in the front-right corner. The sign sits on and intersects the awning, the awning clips into the bay, and the sign nearly collides with the upper window box. Silhouettes merge instead of separating.
The awning stripes render as fragmented, jagged blocks with gaps, which reads as a geometry glitch rather than a scalloped canvas awning.
The hero element is undersized. The shop occupies only half of one ground-floor facade, so at kit or thumbnail scale this reads as a generic house rather than a bakery.

In the dark brand probe the walls stay light grey-blue, so the probe does not produce a darker scheme. The lime awning also clashes against the periwinkle roof, so the awning role mapping lacks harmony control.
In the 3-floor render the shopfront stays the same small cluster, so the added height makes the bakery read as even more incidental.
The renders shown cannot verify the lights knob, and the sign colour has little visible effect because the sign stays wood-yellow in every render.
grades.lesson: The signature element named in the brief must be modelled as a distinct, unoccluded silhouette that reads at thumbnail size, with clearance from neighbouring parts. Check the asset at 128px: if the product type can't be named from the silhouette alone, the hero feature needs to be bigger, simpler, or moved.

flaws: The hero element fails the brief. The 'big bread-shaped sign' is built from stacked rectangular slabs with plank-like scoring. It reads as a pile of lumber, not a loaf, and in the Pistachio preset its brown tone makes it look exactly like a woodpile on the roof.
The bay window of loaves is not legible. It is a shallow recessed box with tiny brown blobs on shelves that turn to mush at normal viewing size, and there is no visible bay projection.
The striped awning is chopped into small isometric segments that crowd into the window frame and sign band. The stripes read as noise rather than a clear canopy.
Small coloured tabs float on the shop's right side wall in every render (red, blue or teal depending on preset). They look like stray or misplaced geometry, not intentional detail.
The chimney smoke is a stack of hard-edged white discs. It reads as a stacked object, not smoke, and sits awkwardly on the chimney.
The shop extension's ground-floor detail is much denser than the clean, flat main house. The two parts feel like they were made at different levels of detail.
At max floors the house works and the window boxes appear. However, the side-wall fragments, cramped awning and woodpile sign carry over unchanged, so nothing improves at range.
The dark brand probe only shifts walls to a muted slate. The lit windows and sign stay saturated yellow and dominate, but the result is not broken.
grades.lesson: The element that names an asset (here the bread sign) must read from its silhouette alone at thumbnail size. Model it with the characteristic profile (a domed, rounded loaf) rather than assembling it from stacked boxes. Check it in a flat single-colour render before adding surface detail.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A four-to-six storey apartment block with balconies and plants, a lobby door and rooftop water tank. Knobs: wall, balcony colour, floors 3-7, width 4-6 m, water tank toggle, lights.

flaws: Brand probes recolour the foliage. Plants become salmon cubes in the light probe and purple cubes in the dark probe, so they no longer read as plants. The brief explicitly calls for 'balconies and plants'.

Dark brand probe inverts the value structure. The roof and parapet turn near-white over black walls, and the lime balconies overpower everything. The building reads as a broken render, not a dark-themed asset.
Lobby canopy and door nearly vanish in the dark probe, so the entrance loses its focal point.
Water tank is the same saturated blue in every render, including defaults, Harbour and both probes. It is never integrated into the palette and clashes with the Oasis town tone at defaults.
Preset 'Terracotta' is pixel-identical to defaults, which wastes a preset slot.
At max floors and width, the balcony stack becomes a dense, repetitive grid of red boxes and planters. Rows visually overlap, the facade reads as clutter, and the ground-floor entrance is buried.
Left facade window pattern (lit/unlit) repeats identically per floor, so it looks mechanical rather than lived-in.
Width knob is barely perceptible at max; the building mostly grows taller and is scaled down to fit the frame.
grades.lesson: When mapping brand colours onto an illustrative asset, bind them only to designated accent surfaces (trim, balconies, awnings). Keep semantic materials like foliage, water and glass on fixed or tightly constrained hues. Also preserve the value hierarchy between roof, walls and accents, so any brand palette still reads as the same object.

flaws: Right-hand facade has no consistent storey rhythm. Balconies in the two bays sit at staggered heights that don't line up with floor lines or with the left face's window rows, so the building reads as jumbled rather than as stacked apartments.
Balcony railings and planters cut across the middles of tall windows. Small red-framed door/window shapes float between balconies, so it is unclear what is a door, a window or a railing.
At max floors the clutter compounds. Balconies crowd and overlap one another on the right face, windows are half-hidden behind rails, and the facade turns into visual noise.
Shutters on the left face appear sporadically (one pair at defaults, scattered pairs at max) with no logic, which reads as a random-placement artifact.
The lobby is undersized and cramped. The door is a sliver squeezed under a striped awning between two planters, so the ground floor reads weaker than the brief's 'lobby door' calls for.
Dark brand probe maps balconies to saturated lime against cool grey-blue walls. The result is garish, and the lime planter boxes collide with the green plant accents, losing the plants.
The building occupies a small fraction of the frame with large empty margins, which makes the fine facade detail hard to read at thumbnail scale.
Width knob effect is hard to discern across renders. At max the footprint looks barely different, so the 4-6 m width range seems to deliver little visible change.
grades.lesson: Place every facade element (windows, balconies, doors, shutters, planters) from one shared floor-height and bay grid so they all snap to the same storey lines and bay centres; never let a protruding element overlap an opening, and verify the rhythm holds at the maximum floor and width counts.

flaws: The lobby entrance canopy collides with the lowest balcony on the right face at defaults. Both shapes overlap in the same screen space instead of reading as separate architectural elements.

At max floors and width, the balcony stack on the right face becomes a dense, overlapping tangle of slabs, railings and plants. The lowest balcony fuses into the canopy, and the facade reads as clutter rather than rhythm.
The balcony top rails and posts read as floating diagonal sticks detached from the slabs, especially at the upper balconies, which makes the railing construction look broken.
In the dark brand probe, the balcony colour is a pale green that sits at low contrast against the pale lavender wall. The balconies wash out and the scheme looks muddy rather than branded.
The lights knob has no visible effect in any render. Every window is lit yellow everywhere, so its range cannot be judged and it looks non-functional.
The width knob (4-6 m) produces almost no perceptible change in footprint or window count at max, so the knob adds little control for the designer.
The left facade window grid stays a fixed two columns regardless of width, so wider blocks just get emptier walls instead of more bays.
grades.lesson: When a repeated element (balconies, windows, signage) is stacked by a count knob alongside a one-off feature (entrance canopy, lobby door), reserve an explicit clearance zone for the one-off. Derive the repeat placement from that zone so the two can never intersect at any knob value, and verify the collision at both min and max counts before submitting.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A narrow ramen shop with noren curtain strips over the door, a vertical sign and paper lanterns that glow. Knobs: wall, curtain colour, lantern count 0-4, roof gable/flat, lights.

flaws: Dark brand probe: walls go pure black and the roof near-white, so the isometric face shading collapses. The left wall and front facade are almost indistinguishable, the white roof planes barely separate, and the building reads as a flat silhouette rather than a 3D block.
Dark brand probe also turns the noren and lanterns lime green and the sign cyan. The palette loses its ramen-shop identity and no longer matches the town-shop palette the brief requires.
The 'Shoyu' preset renders identically to the defaults, so the preset is wasted.
At maximum, four lanterns crowd under the awning and overlap each other. The vertical sign floats awkwardly mid-facade on the taller building instead of anchoring to the shopfront.
Lanterns do not visibly glow in any render: no halo or emissive falloff. They read as small coloured cylinders, which misses a core point of the brief.
The vertical sign holds blank dark squares with no glyph or character suggestion, so it reads as a generic panel rather than a ramen sign.
Side-wall windows are flat blue-grey rectangles with no frame or mullion detail. This is inconsistent with the detailed front windows.
grades.lesson: When brand colours drive surfaces with directional face shading, compute each face's tone relative to the input's luminance and clamp it to a usable range. Near-black or near-white brand inputs must still yield clearly separated top, left and right faces, otherwise 3D forms collapse into flat silhouettes.

flaws: At every range knob's maximum the four lanterns pile into a tangled cluster at the right end of the awning. They overlap each other and crowd into the vertical sign, which is a broken render.

Even at defaults the three lanterns hang across the awning edge and door rather than sitting in a clean, evenly spaced row. The composition of the shopfront, the asset's hero element, feels cramped and unresolved.
The noren curtain strips named in the brief are barely readable. The door shows only a faint coloured band, not distinct split fabric strips, so the defining ramen-shop cue is weak.
The lanterns are meant to glow but have no visible glow, halo or emissive contrast against the facade in any render, including the dark brand probe.

In the dark brand probe the sign becomes hot pink with low-contrast purple glyphs and the lanterns wash out to tan. The palette mapping loses the red-lantern identity and looks garish rather than on-brand.
The large blank left side wall carries only an AC unit and two small windows, so at defaults the massing reads as a generic suburban house more than a narrow ramen shop.
The pseudo-glyph marks on the sign read as fake text. A designer shipping this in a product with Japanese-speaking users could be embarrassed by them.
grades.lesson: When a count knob adds repeated elements, derive their spacing from the host surface's real width and clamp the maximum count to what fits. Then verify the max render shows no instances overlapping each other or neighbouring features.

flaws: The brief's headline feature, noren curtain strips over the door, does not read in any render. The door area shows lanterns under a plain awning, so the curtain colour knob has no visible effect across presets or brand probes.
The vertical sign sits on the far side face and is mostly hidden by the building edge. Its glyphs are illegible coloured blobs. In the Shoyu preset it goes nearly dark and loses its glow.
The asset does not read as a ramen shop at thumbnail size. Without noren or a legible sign, it reads as a generic two-storey townhouse with lanterns.
At max range, four lanterns crowd under the short awning and overlap each other and the awning edge. The entrance becomes cluttered and cramped.
In the dark brand probe, the roof turns a pale, washed-out periwinkle that sits close to the background in value. The silhouette weakens, and the probe reads lighter rather than darker.
The lower brown timber storey never responds to the brand or presets. Combined with the barely changing yellow sign, the house looks like a single colourway with a recoloured roof.
The small window on the right side face is cut off at the corner edge in defaults and presets, so it looks like a clipping mistake rather than an intended detail.
Brand probes and presets differ almost only in roof hue, so the range is shallow. The wall knob barely shifts the upper storey.
grades.lesson: Before submitting, list every named feature in the brief and confirm each one is clearly visible and identifiable from the default camera at thumbnail size. A signature element that is occluded or missing makes both the asset and its knob worthless.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A park bench with a slatted seat and back, optional planter boxes at each end. Footprint 2x1. Knobs: wood colour, frame colour, planters toggle, length 1.5-3 m.

warnings: colour knobs without a brand role: wood, flowers

flaws: Bench structure is incomplete. The front-right leg is missing in every render, so the front stretcher rail ends in mid-air over the plinth, and the right end of the seat has no visible support. This is especially clear in the backless render.
The bench's side rails clip through the planter boxes. Short green bar stubs poke out of the front faces of both planters (left planter lower face, right planter side face) in every render.
The front-left leg collides with the left planter's rim instead of sitting cleanly beside it or butting against it.
Preset 'Park' is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it adds no variation.
Foliage reads as crude stacked cylinders. The flowers are flat sugar-cube blocks perched on top, one of them half-buried behind the bush. Detail quality falls below the bench itself.
At maximum length the planters and plinth render visibly smaller than at defaults. This suggests the whole piece is rescaled to fit instead of extended, which breaks the brief's fixed 6 m kit scale.
Planters take the wood colour. In the dark brand probe this gives saturated purple boxes, and in the light brand probe orange-red boxes, which look unintentional next to the untinted green bushes.
The planters toggle and the minimum length (1.5 m) are not shown in any render, so two of the four briefed knobs cannot be verified.
grades.lesson: Build multi-part objects from shared anchor points. Every structural member, such as a leg, rail or slat, should end on a support, and separate sub-assemblies should never interpenetrate. Before shipping, render each optional part on its own and check for floating ends and clipping.

flaws: The frame does not read as a structure. In the defaults, a frame-coloured rail lies flat on the base plate in front of the seat. It is anchored only by one short post at the front-left. Its right end stops in mid-air short of the right planter. It looks like a dropped stick, not a stretcher or leg.
The seat has no visible legs or supports apart from that single front-left post. It appears to float between the planters.
The backrest has a frame post at the left end but almost nothing at the right end. Only a sliver of dark frame shows behind the planter, so the back looks unsupported.

At max length, a small orphan frame-coloured block floats in the gap between seat and backrest at mid-span. Mid legs appear under the seat, but the stray ground rail is still there. The structure gets more confusing as length increases, not more coherent.
With back set to backless, the lone front post and ground rail remain. This leaves an obvious leftover part with no purpose.

The planter boxes stay a hard-coded terracotta in every preset and both brand probes. Only the wood, frame and flower accents follow the brand. In the dark probe, grey frame plus terracotta plus cyan flowers reads as three unrelated palettes.
The flower blossoms are loose cubes, some sitting off the shrub on the soil. At thumbnail scale they read as noise rather than flowers.
Planters toggled off was not shown, so the briefed planters knob cannot be verified. The extra back choice is welcome, but it exposes the orphaned-geometry bug.
grades.lesson: Derive every structural member (legs, stretchers, posts) from the geometry it supports, so it moves, scales and disappears with that geometry. Then inspect each part in every render and ask what it touches and what it holds up. Any piece that ends in mid-air or survives a toggle that removed its purpose is a bug, not a detail.

flaws: Parts do not connect. The backrest is offset from the seat. Its left post overhangs the seat toward the left planter, and its right end runs into the right planter. The bench reads as stacked boxes, not one assembled object.

The seat's right end stops short in open space near the right planter, while its left end butts into the left planter. The piece is asymmetric in a way that looks like a placement bug, not a design choice.
Small detached green leg or bracket stubs sit in front of the left planter at every setting, including backless. They read as stray geometry.

Scale is inconsistent across the length knob. At maximum length the planters, flowers and frame shrink while the base plate stays the same size. A block-kit piece needs constant real-world units, so it will not tile or match neighbouring kit pieces.

Scale looks wrong for the brief. A 1.5–3 m bench should occupy a small part of a 2x1 tile on the 6 m grid (12 × 6 m). Here the bench and oversized planters fill nearly the whole plate, so it will not match town-shop scale.
The flower clusters are chunky and uniform, and dominate the silhouette. The bench, which is the subject, gets visually crowded out by the planters.
Brand probes and colour presets recolour cleanly, but they only hide the structural problems; none of the renders fix the alignment issues.
grades.lesson: For modular kit pieces, build every component from one fixed unit system anchored to shared attachment points (posts, rails, edges). Do not scale or position components independently. Then check the extreme knob values to confirm that parts still meet, nothing floats or interpenetrates, and the object's real-world size relative to the grid tile never changes.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A bus stop shelter with a roof, glass back panel, bench, timetable sign and a pole sign. Footprint 3x2. Knobs: frame colour, roof colour, sign colour, lights.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: lights

flaws: Preset 'Kyoto' is pixel-identical to the defaults. Either the preset is not wired up or it duplicates the default values, so it offers the buyer nothing.

The 'lights' knob has no visible effect. The pale yellow strip under the roof looks the same in every render, including with every range knob at its maximum, so a brief-listed knob is effectively dead.
The pole sign's glyphs are tiny smudged marks that read as noise rather than a bus icon or route number.
The brief asks for a timetable sign, but there is no clearly identifiable timetable on the shelter.
The 'glass' side panel renders as an opaque slate-blue slab with no transparency or reflection cue, so it does not read as glass. The back panel is only faintly distinguishable.

In the dark brand probe, the lime frame against the lavender roof is garish. The frame colour is applied flat to every member with no shading tone shift, so saturated brand colours lose the isometric depth the defaults have.
Even at maximum, the range knobs only slightly widen the shelter and bench. The variation is too small to justify a range knob.
At defaults the composition is competent but generic. The roof slab is a plain inset rectangle with little detail, and the piece would not stand out in a paid kit.
grades.lesson: Before submitting, compare every preset and every knob's extreme values against the default render. If any preset or knob produces no visible change, wire it up properly or remove it.

flaws: The glass back panel has a jagged, stair-stepped edge in every render. It reads as cracked or broken glass, or as a rendering artifact, not as a reflection. It is the first thing the eye lands on inside the shelter.

With roofStyle 'pitched', the cream light bar still sits on the outer face of the front slope. It floats on the roof instead of mounting under the eave as a canopy light. The light was not re-anchored when the roof geometry changed.
Even on the flat roof, a cream light strip lies on top of the roof next to the dark panel, duplicating the one under the fascia. A shelter light on the roof's upper surface makes no sense.

With every range knob at maximum, the shelter grows taller but the yellow timetable/ad panel keeps its height. This leaves a glass sliver above it at top-left that looks like a leftover gap. The widened shelter also crowds the pole sign: the right post and roof corner nearly collide with it.

The large yellow side panel never responds to sign or brand colour. In the dark brand probe it sits against a lime frame and lavender roof, and the combination looks garish rather than branded. Only the panel's small header strip adopts the brand colour.
The 'lights' knob has no visible effect in any supplied render, so its value cannot be verified.
The roofStyle variant also shifts the whole composition and the pole position relative to the base. That risks grid misalignment for a kit piece meant to snap to a 6 m grid.
grades.lesson: Every decorative mark (reflection, light strip, trim) must be computed from and clipped to the surface it decorates, and must read unambiguously at thumbnail size. A jagged reflection reads as a crack, and a light left behind when its parent surface changes shape will float.

flaws: At every range knob's maximum, a pale glass pane pokes out above the frame header at the top-left, between the timetable panel and the roof. It reads as geometry clipping through the roof overhang.

At maximum, the solar panel pair sits off-centre on the enlarged roof, drifting toward the back-left. The roof also visibly detaches from the frame, so the roof parts are not anchored to shared dimensions.
The pole-sign glyph is a speech-bubble shape that reads as a chat or message icon, not a bus. Communicating 'bus stop' is the core job of this piece, and it fails at a glance.
The timetable and ad panel faces are rows of crude grey dashes. At this size they look like placeholder rather than designed detail.
At defaults the large side panel hides most of the bench. One of the four required brief elements is barely legible unless the max extreme is used.
The dark brand probe renders pastel lime, lavender and light cyan. That pairing is garish, and the probe gives no evidence the kit holds together with a genuinely dark brand palette.
The 'lights' knob has no visible effect in any render beyond a thin yellow header strip and the lamp cap, so its usefulness cannot be confirmed.
The shelter is crammed onto the left of the slab with an empty band of tiles in front. Composition on the 3x2 footprint feels unbalanced rather than planned.
grades.lesson: When a knob resizes a parent part (roof, base, frame), derive every attached child (panels, glass, decals, fixtures) from the same computed dimensions and anchor points rather than fixed offsets, then render the max extreme to confirm nothing drifts, floats or pokes through.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A boxy toy hatchback car with windows, wheels as dark cylinders lying sideways (use boxes for wheels), headlights. Footprint 4x2. Knobs: body colour (primary), roof rack toggle, lights.

warnings: knobs with very subtle effect: lights

flaws: Roof rack rails float above the roof on disconnected posts. One rail passes over the cargo box edge and another hangs unsupported at the rear left, so the rack reads as broken geometry, not a toy accessory.

The side window panels are offset from the body and stand proud of it. At max length the near-side window slab sticks out past the body silhouette, and the panes do not align with the door or pillar seams.
The silhouette reads as a boxy SUV/jeep with a raised roof box, not the hatchback the brief asked for. There is no sloped or distinct rear hatch.
The wheels are tall dark slabs bolted outside the body with white squares. They read as speaker boxes more than wheels, and they look disproportionately large against the 4x2 footprint.
Headlights are a single small orange tab on the far corner. They are barely visible from the canonical view, and no render demonstrates the 'lights' knob doing anything.
Preset 'Sky' is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it adds no range. The preset name 'Tram' is also nonsensical for a car.
In pickup style, a grey slab floats on top of the cab cargo box. This is roof-rack geometry left over from the hatchback that no longer fits the shape.
At max range the body stretches into a limo, while the roof box and rails keep their size and drift off-centre. The roof accessories do not scale or re-anchor with the body.
grades.lesson: Anchor every accessory (racks, rails, panels, windows) to the parent surface it attaches to. Derive its position and size from that parent's current dimensions, so it stays seated and in proportion when other knobs change shape or style.

flaws: Doesn't read as a hatchback: the long flat hood, tall upright cabin and squared tail give a sedan/SUV silhouette, missing the brief's archetype.
Wheels read as dark crates bolted to the outside of the body rather than wheels under it. Only the near-side pair is visible, and they jut out past the fenders as if glued on.
Roof rack's long grey bar runs diagonally down across the side window and windshield area, cutting through glass instead of sitting on the roof.
Thin grey trim rods (side rails, door handles, mirror arms) float off the body surfaces, which looks like z-fighting or detached geometry and makes the model look cluttered.
Front face is asymmetric: one lit orange headlight beside an unexplained dark rectangle, so it looks like a missing headlight rather than a design choice.
At max knob values the roof rack slab shifts off-centre and the rack bars detach and float above and in front of the roof. Accessories are not re-anchored when body dimensions change.
In the 5-door variant the added third window and door seam collide with the side trim rail, cramming the rear quarter.
Dark brand probe produced a bright lime body with navy trim. There is no dark-brand result, which suggests brand colours map to the wrong role.
The light car body uses a single flat tint per face with little value separation between the cabin and lower body, so in light brands the shapes merge.
grades.lesson: Position every accessory and detail part from the parent body's computed dimensions (never fixed offsets), then render at knob extremes to confirm each part stays seated on its host surface with no floating or interpenetrating geometry.

flaws: The roof is an incoherent pile of overlapping white slabs at mismatched heights, with a cream trim edge and stray grey bars. It reads as debris, not as a cabin roof, and it dominates the silhouette at defaults and in every preset.
The windows are flat grey panels standing proud of the body. The front 'windshield' looks like a detached slab leaning off the cabin rather than glazing set into it.
The body reads as a boxy SUV or wagon, not the hatchback the brief asked for. There is no clear sloped or short rear hatch.
The wheels are barely legible as wheels. They read as dark bumper blocks at the corners, and their placement and proportions don't sell 'cylinder lying sideways'.
Dark brand probe is broken: some roof slabs flip to charcoal while others stay white, so a single surface becomes a striped patchwork. Palette roles are not assigned consistently across parts.
At max range the roof collapses into one flat white lid with the bars on top. This reads better than the defaults, which shows the default geometry is the weaker state.
The 'doors' choice knob (5-door) produces a near-invisible change, only a shifted seam line. It is not worth exposing as a knob.
The headlight and lights knob has no visible effect in any render. The front lamp is a small orange tile that reads as an indicator, not a headlight.
grades.lesson: Block out the core silhouette from a few clearly separated volumes (body, cabin, wheels) and confirm it reads as the named object at thumbnail size before adding detail. Never stack overlapping slabs at slightly different heights on one surface: it reads as clutter and breaks palette mapping.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A food truck with a serving hatch, awning flap, menu board and a little roof sign. Footprint 5x2.5. Knobs: body colour, awning colour, sign colour, hatch open toggle, lights.

flaws: The 'every range knob at maximum' render is pixel-identical to defaults. The range knobs either do nothing visible or do not exist, so the lights and hatch-open controls from the brief show no effect anywhere.
The Classic preset is identical to defaults, so it adds nothing.
The menu board required by the brief is not visible in any render.
Wheel placement reads wrong. The rear axle sits roughly mid-body under the hatch, leaving a long unsupported rear overhang with a grey slab hanging beneath it.
The side rail and bumper geometry looks loose and detached. The rear end shows open, empty door frames and a stray vertical pole that read as unfinished rather than intentional.

In the dark brand probe the sign box turns translucent cyan against lime-green trim on a grey body. The result is a garish, clashing palette, and the sign colour's mapping to brand tokens is not controlled.
The coffee variant's cup is undersized relative to the sign tray and has a dull grey lid, so it reads weaker than the burger.
Overall the piece looks like a decent sketch, but its construction details are not polished enough for a paid kit.
grades.lesson: Before submitting, diff each knob's extreme render against the default render. If a declared knob (toggle, range or light) produces no visible change, it is broken or missing, and the asset must not ship until every knob in the brief demonstrably does something.

flaws: The free-standing A-frame menu sign sits inside the rear wheel and bumper block at the front-left corner instead of standing clear on the ground. It intersects geometry in every render, including the max-range one, where it overlaps even more.
The wheels read as hollow square boxes, especially the right-hand wheel with its white inner square. They look like crates bolted under the chassis rather than wheels, even in a voxel idiom.
The cab is hard to read. The grey cab roof floats behind the main roof as a flat slab, the side mirror is a detached grey bar, and at max range the cab collapses to a thin sliver.

Dark brand probe: the brand colour is applied to the sign box as saturated cyan with a pale inset. The yellow burger sitting on it clashes. The grey body also loses contrast against the pale blue-grey background, so the silhouette goes muddy.
Range knobs at maximum barely change the asset beyond small proportional shifts. The ranges are either too timid or the knobs don't drive anything meaningful.
The brief asks for a hatch-open toggle and lights, but no closed-hatch or lights-on render is shown. These knobs cannot be verified and may be missing or broken.
The presets (Tram, Harbour) are only trim recolours of the same truck. There is little variety for a kit piece.
grades.lesson: When a builder places a secondary prop (a sign, bench or bin) next to a main body, compute its position from the body's full outer bounds including wheels, bumpers and overhangs, plus a fixed clearance gap. Re-check that clearance at every knob extreme, so the prop never intersects the model it accompanies.

flaws: The front-left corner is cluttered. The counter end, condiment bottles, red tail light, pale bumper step and wheel all pile into about 40px, and the silhouette turns to mush at the point where the eye lands first. At max range the longer counter crowds this corner even further.
The cab is underdesigned. The front is a flat grey pane with no headlights, grille or clear windshield, so the truck reads as a box with a stub on the end, not a vehicle.
The pale grey bumper slab under the rear looks like an unfinished plinth. It does not read as a bumper or a step, and it stays the same stark value in every colourway.
The 'lights' knob from the brief produces no visible element in any render: no headlamps, no marquee bulbs, no glow. A buyer cannot tell what it does.
Framing is off-centre. The truck sits low-left with a large empty band on the right and top, which is awkward for a drop-in asset.
The roof stays bright white in the dark brand probe and dominates the grey body. The probe recolours only accents, so the dark brand never feels owned.
grades.lesson: Distribute small details across a silhouette rather than letting several of them converge at one corner. Then check that every briefed knob has a visible effect at its default, because a knob that changes nothing reads as broken.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A red telephone booth with glass panes and a lit crown sign. Footprint 1x1. Knobs: colour, lights.

flaws: Roof = 'pitched' is broken. The crown plinth is set at the old stepped-roof height, so the hip roof's ridge and back slopes rise behind and through it. The slopes also have an inconsistent lit triangle on the right that reads as a geometry error, not shading.
At max range knobs the base shrinks and the booth goes tall and thin. This breaks the 1x1 footprint on the 6 m grid that the brief requires, so the piece no longer lines up with other kit pieces.
The header signs, the booth's main identifying feature, are dark L-shaped blocks that read as mail slots, not a 'TELEPHONE' sign or any legible sign glyph.
The 'lit crown sign' is a large solid gold crown sculpture, not a sign, and it is oversized for the cap. It dominates the silhouette at every setting.
The lights knob shows no visible change across the renders. The glazing stays the same flat cream-yellow, so the 'lit' state isn't communicated.
Dark brand probe: lime frame against cream and yellow glazing is low contrast. The stepped roof tiers and mullions nearly merge, and the cyan crown looks off-palette next to the rest of the kit.
The presets are plain recolours (terracotta and green), and the names 'Pillar' and 'Tram' don't describe what changes. They add no real range.
The glazing is flat fill with no interior hint (no handset or shelf), and the front corner post is thin and indistinct where the two faces meet.
grades.lesson: When a choice knob swaps a base shape (roof type, cap, top), compute where dependent parts attach from the selected shape's actual top surface, not from a fixed height. Render every choice option, not just the defaults, before submitting.

flaws: Gable roof variant is broken. A stray third crown emblem floats on the left roof slope, a leftover from the flat/stepped roof, so the decoration was not re-anchored to the new geometry.
Gable roof reads as lopsided. The finial sits at the end of the ridge rather than centred, and the slope proportions look accidental rather than designed.
At the max-range render the stepped roof tiers and finial shift relative to the cornice, so the cap looks slightly off-centre on the taller, slimmer body.
Interior telephone details (dark box and grey bar) are drawn across the glazing bars on the left face, which reads as a depth-sorting error rather than an object seen through glass.
The 'Post Red & Gold' preset is pixel-identical to the defaults, so it adds no value as a preset.
The brief lists a 'lights' knob, but no render shows the crown sign or panes changing state; the glass is always lit, so the knob's effect cannot be verified.
The dark brand probe recolours the body to lime and turns the crown and finial cyan, losing the warm sign that makes the object read as a lit telephone booth.
Niche usefulness: a single decorative town prop with only colour and roof knobs gives limited reuse for professional product work.
grades.lesson: Whenever a choice knob swaps a base shape (roof, top, cap), re-anchor or hide every ornament attached to the old shape, and render every choice value before submitting, so leftover decorations don't float on the new geometry.

flaws: The crown sign is the booth's signature detail, but its glyph does not read as a crown. It looks like a blocky trident or cactus in every render.
The horizontal glazing bars look like ladder rungs stuck onto the panes. They cross the vertical mullions as raised slats, so the faces read as grilles, not small-paned K6 glazing.
Door handles appear on two faces, and on the left face the handle sits in the middle of the glass instead of on a frame stile. A booth has one hinged door, so this reads as a modelling error.
In the dark brand probe, the lime body and glazing bars nearly vanish against the yellow lit panes. The window grid loses its definition.
The light brand probe turns the crown glyph a muddy olive that is barely distinguishable from the sign fill.
At max knobs the roof stack gets cramped, and the finial looks pinched into the top cap instead of sitting on it.
The dome roof is stacked octagonal discs on a square slab, which reads more like a wedding cake than the curved K6 roof it implies.
No render shows the 'lights' knob in its off state, so the night/unlit look cannot be verified. The visible range seems to change only proportions and hue.
grades.lesson: When an asset's identity rests on a small iconographic detail (a crest, glyph or logo), design it as a simplified, recognisable silhouette at the actual rendered pixel size. Check that it stays legible against every possible fill colour. An unreadable signature detail makes the whole asset look generic.

brief: Oasis Town 3D block kit piece on the 6 m grid, matching town-shop.mjs scale and palette. A pair of vending machines with lit fronts and rows of coloured drinks. Footprint 2x1. Knobs: machine colours, machines 1-3, lights.

flaws: The last machine in the row is missing its lower front body in every render. Below its shelf window there is only a grey bar, then bare white base. Its dispensing slot floats on the floor plate with nothing behind it. This happens at defaults, in all presets, in both brand probes, and on the third machine at max.
The rear machine's side panel reads as a thin, washed-out slab with no volume. Its roof also overhangs further back than its neighbour's. The pair looks like one solid machine beside a hollow shell.
The brief asks for 'rows of coloured drinks', but each shelf holds only one or two cans. The machines read as mostly empty. On the rear machine the cans cluster against the left wall.
The fronts do not read as lit. The window interiors are flat pale yellow with no glow, emission or contrast change. The 'lights' knob shows no visible effect in any render.
At max with 3 machines, the base plate extends past the right machine as an empty white apron. The footprint and base do not scale cleanly with machine count.

Smaller detailing is crude for a paid kit piece: a flat white stripe on the side, three vent slots, and a coin bar with two blobs. Next to the blocky shelves, this falls short of a polished town-kit standard.
grades.lesson: When geometry is built per instance in a loop, render and inspect every instance at every count setting, not just the first or hero one. A part that only gets built for some instances (here, the missing lower body) breaks the asset in every render.

flaws: At the default count of 2 machines, a ghost third machine is left behind on the right. Its dark roof slab, button cluster and green label float beside a translucent, unshaded body. The artefact appears in the defaults, in both presets and in both brand probes, so the shipping state is visibly broken.
The 3-machine render is clean, which shows the count knob hides only some of each machine's parts. The leftover parts read as a glitch, not as a design choice.
The base plinth and the white kerb strip run out past the two visible machines toward the ghost slot, so the footprint looks misaligned with what is drawn.

The drink stock is hard-coded to the same multicolour set and does not follow the palette. In the Blossom preset and the dark brand probe the drinks clash with the machine colours instead of feeling art-directed.
The lights knob produces no visible difference in any render, so I cannot confirm it does anything. The 'lit fronts' in the brief do not read as lit at defaults.

The side ad panel and the front detailing are decent at this scale. However, the cabinet bodies are flat single-tone slabs with a little hard edge shading. The polish is below the town-shop kit pieces this piece is meant to match.
grades.lesson: When a count or visibility knob removes an instance, gate every sub-part of that instance (roof, trim, buttons, labels, base segments) through one shared visibility check. Then render every discrete count value, not just the maximum, before submitting.

flaws: The drink display reads as visual noise, not 'rows of coloured drinks'. Dozens of tiny white cubes with coloured caps are jittered at inconsistent heights and depths. At the kit's viewing scale it looks like a pile of rubble behind glass, not orderly shelved cans or bottles.
Several drink cubes on the left edge of each window appear to poke past the dark glass frame, breaking the frame line.

The brief asks for 'lit fronts', but nothing glows in any render. No emissive panel, light spill, or contrast lift on the glass is visible. The fronts read as unlit, and no render shows the lights knob doing anything visible.

The cream ground mat sits only in front of the first machine (and two of three machines at max). The base slab also overhangs the right side further than the left. Both read as placement errors rather than intent.
The side panel graphic (two coloured squares in a frame) is generic and does not clearly say 'vending machine' or 'advert'. It adds little.
At 3 machines the third reverts to colour 1. That is acceptable, but there is no third colour knob, so the triple can only alternate.
grades.lesson: Repeated small detail (stock, windows, foliage) must be laid out on a strict, regular grid with a few large, legible units, and checked at the asset's real thumbnail size. Dense jittered micro-geometry turns into noise. Any 'lit'/state knob must produce a visibly different render, or it is not a real knob.
